Research / Substance use and the 2024 vote

Substance use and the 2024 vote

NSDUH substate rates · one regression

One point of past-month marijuana use lines up with +1.48 points of Democratic two-party share on the vote-weighted fit. Alcohol’s fit is +1.10 per point. After log density and age, marijuana is +1.13 and alcohol is +0.66. At the 10th percentile of regional marijuana use the fitted share is 43.7%. At the 90th it is 55.4%.

The study in eight charts

Scores, IQ, the vote, and the laws, each from the data files on this page. Every chart is labeled measured or predicted, and the detailed sections follow. Psychosis, dependence, withdrawal anger, and violence are in their own section further down.

1 · Test scores

Grade 8 math is down 11.4 points from its 2013 high, and every NAEP series is lower in 2024

Y · NAEP points vs. the 2013 national scoreX · Test year

Measured. NAEP national public composite means, NCES. Change from 2013: math 8 −11.4, reading 8 −9.4, reading 4 −6.4, math 4 −3.9. The green band is the period in which states began legalizing adult use. The decline started before the 2020 school closures and deepened after them. Raw scores and the law timeline.

2 · Every state

Grade 8 math fell in 51 of 51 jurisdictions. States with legal adult use fell further on all four tests

Adult use legal by 2024 (25)Not legal (26)

Y · Test and adult-use status in 2024X · NAEP points, 2024 minus 2013

Measured. Each dot is a state or DC; the bar is the unweighted average. Differences, legal minus not legal: math, grade 8 −3.4 (SE 1.2); reading, grade 8 −1.8 (SE 1.1); math, grade 4 −3.4 (SE 1.2); reading, grade 4 −2.9 (SE 1.4). Legal states also differ in other ways, including how long schools stayed remote in 2020–21, so this is a comparison, not an effect estimate. The within-state first difference is further down.

3 · IQ

Persistent users lost IQ points, and the loss was still there at 38 and at 45

Measured, DunedinPredicted from potencyAll U.S. adults, any cause

Y · Study and populationX · IQ points lower

The two Dunedin bars are measured in the same people, compared with their own childhood IQ (n = 1,037 cohort; 86 long-term users at 45). Meier 2012: cessation “did not fully restore” functioning among adolescent-onset users. Meier 2022: deficits were absent or smaller among those who quit. The dashed bar is this page’s potency prediction, not a measurement (model). The grey bar is the published ICAR35 slope for all U.S. adults, any cause, at 15 IQ points per SD. Meier et al., PNAS 2012, 10.1073/pnas.1206820109; Meier et al., Am J Psychiatry 2022, 10.1176/appi.ajp.2021.21060664; Dworak et al., Intelligence 2023, 10.1016/j.intell.2023.101734.

4 · The vote

The Democratic share climbs from 41.9% to 60.0% across marijuana-use quintiles

Y · 2024 Democratic two-party share, %X · Past-month marijuana use, quintile of 382 regions

Measured. Vote-weighted mean share in each fifth of NSDUH 2021–2023 substate regions, about 30 million two-party votes per bar. Density and education also rise across the quintiles; after density and age the slope is +1.13 points of share per point of use (table). This is an area-level association, not individual voters.

5 · Over time

After legalization, states shifted toward Democrats: +0.5 points one election later, +4.2 points 3 elections later

Y · State minus national Democratic share, change in pointsX · Years from the election in or before the legalization year

Measured. Presidential two-party share 2004–2024 for the 25 adult-use jurisdictions, each relative to the national share and to its own value at the election in or before its legalization year. Before legalization the line stays within 0.4 points of zero. Later points cover fewer states, led by the 2012–2014 legalizers (Colorado, Washington, Alaska, Oregon, DC); whiskers are 95% intervals across states. The shift is consistent with legalization changing who lives and votes there, and also with states that were already trending Democratic choosing to legalize.

6 · Who passed it

To end federal marijuana prohibition, 97–99% of House Democrats voted yes. Republicans: 1–3%

DemocratsRepublicans

Y · House passage voteX · Share of the party’s members voting yes

Measured. House Clerk roll calls; members not voting are left out. The 2018 Farm Bill is the only one of these to become law. Both MORE Act votes would have removed marijuana from the Controlled Substances Act, and drew 5 Republican yes votes in 2020 and 3 in 2022. Every act and its roll call.

7 · Who enacted it

Voters passed 38 of the 76 laws that eased access. Democratic signers enacted 26, Republican signers 9

Voters, ballot initiativeSigned by a DemocratSigned by a RepublicanLaw without signature or over a vetoNot recorded

Y · Kind of lawX · Share of laws, count on the bar

Measured. Laws in force that eased access: state medical and adult-use programs, the federal hemp law, and federal executive actions. Signers are governors, the DC mayor, or the administration that issued the action. Bills that never became law are left out. The full table lists each signer and vote.

8 · State legislatures

Democratic state legislators voted yes 93% of the time, Republicans 49%. On adult use, 6% of Republican votes were yes

DemocraticRepublicanBipartisan, committee, or split controlLaw without signature or over a vetoNot recorded

Y · Who and which lawsX · Share of laws, then share of votes cast yes

Measured. Of 34 state laws passed by a legislature that eased access, Democrats were the prime sponsor of 21 and Republicans of 8; Democratic governors signed 24 and Republican governors 7. Sponsor, signer, chamber majorities, and roll calls come from legislature journals and vote records. The vote bars add every party tally printed for a law, so a legislator who voted on passage and again on a conference report counts twice. Democratic legislators cast 3,109 yes and 245 no votes; Republicans 1,325 and 1,379. Several Republican-majority legislatures passed medical programs, which is where most Republican yes votes are. Each law, sponsor, signer, and vote.

Perception and the vote slope

Group A’s common slope is +0.76 points of Democratic two-party share per point of the rate (clustered SE 0.08). Group B’s is −2.04 (SE 1.03). The difference, group B minus group A, is −2.80 (SE 1.04).

With heroin in group B the difference is −2.39 (SE 1.03). Heroin alone is +8.52 per point (HC1 SE 3.48).

In plain terms: group A is the four substances that alter perception or raise suggestibility in the lab: marijuana, hallucinogens, alcohol, and cocaine. Group B is opioid misuse, pain-reliever misuse, and methamphetamine. Where group A use is higher, the Democratic share is higher. Where group B use is higher, it is not. Green is group A, teal is group B, brown is the gap between them, and a bar that crosses 0 is not distinguishable from no relationship.

Marijuana and test scores

These are not trends over time. Each colored cell is one correlation across states: does a state with more marijuana use have lower scores? Moving right only changes how many years after the use the scores were measured. Red cells mean more use goes with lower scores. Brown cells mean higher scores. Darker is stronger; 0 is no relationship.

The cells are partial correlations, holding log density, age, and education. The most negative is past year marijuana, the 15-year mean, with grade 4 math in the year the exposure window ends: −0.49 (n=98). The strongest positive partial correlation is past month marijuana, the 15-year mean, with grade 8 reading 4 years after the exposure window ends: +0.02 (n=49).

In plain terms: almost every cell in math and grade 4 reading is red, so states with more marijuana use have lower scores after density, age, and education are held equal. The 15-year mean rows are darkest. Grade 8 reading is near 0.

The outcome year is 2019, the latest NAEP year with a full 15-year run of interview-mode pools: the 15-year row is the mean of end years 2005–2019, the 5-year row is the mean of end years 2015–2019, and the latest-pool row is the 2018–2019 estimate, with the 2019–2020 pool absent and the 2021–2024 web-mode pools left out.

Scores are vote-weighted z-scores of the 2019 state means. The composite is the mean of those four z-scores. Democratic share is the 2020 two-party share. Weights are 2020 two-party votes. Partial r residualizes the exposure and the outcome on log density, percent ages 18–25, percent ages 12–17, and bachelor’s share, the vote-weighted region means. Median household income is not in the region file. Alaska and Hawaii are absent from that file, so partial r uses 49 states and Pearson r uses 51. Hallucinogens and opioid misuse begin in the web-mode pools and are off this table. Binge alcohol, illicit drugs other than marijuana, methamphetamine, and pain-reliever misuse have four pre-break pools on the current questionnaire, so only the 2018–2019 row is filled. Heroin’s series starts in 2013–2014, so the 15-year row is omitted. CSV: state_window_correlations.csv.

Use, scores, and the vote over time

National past-month marijuana is 10.8% in the 2018-2019 pool and 15.4% in the 2023-2024 pool. From 2009–2010 to 2018–2019, one more point of past-month marijuana lines up with +0.41 grade-8 mathematics points (SE 0.51).

Past-month marijuana use rose from 4.8% in 2000 to 15.4% in 2024, 3.2 times as high, while alcohol use did not rise

Cumulative and delayed exposure

Past-month marijuana and grade-8 mathematics: −0.02 points per point of use at a lag of 0 years (SE 0.30) and −0.14 at a lag of 8 years (SE 0.30). The same lags on Democratic two-party share are +0.65 (SE 0.26) and +0.10 (SE 0.34).

Past-month alcohol and grade-8 mathematics: +0.19 at lag 0 (SE 0.24) and +0.02 at lag 8 (SE 0.15). A five-year sum of past-month marijuana lines up with −0.01 grade-8 mathematics points per percentage-point-year (SE 0.09). The ten-year sum is −0.02 (SE 0.07).

These are not trends over time. Each dot is a separate within-state regression: the outcome against marijuana or alcohol use measured that many years earlier. Reading left to right compares lags; it does not follow a state through time. Green is past-month marijuana, blue is past-month alcohol.

Children in homes where parents use

Children whose mothers reported cannabis use after learning they were pregnant scored 81.7 on the NIH Toolbox. Children with no prenatal cannabis exposure scored 86.5. Binge prenatal alcohol is Cohen’s d −0.13.

Laboratory results

A suggested false detail was accepted 19% of the time after THC and 8% after placebo. Related-word false alarms were 42% and 27%. Misled responses were 0.25 after alcohol and 0.319 with no alcohol.

Y · Percent of responses

Whiskers: Kloft, 1 SE in percentage points. Gawrylowicz, half the published 95% CI.

Laboratory data, not vote data. Kloft et al. 2020, immediate test, THC versus placebo. Gawrylowicz et al. 2017, alcohol, reverse placebo, and no alcohol.

Suggestibility, predicted from the lab dose

Kloft and colleagues vaporized 300 μg of THC per kilogram, about 21 mg at 70 kg. A suggested false detail was accepted 19% of the time after THC (SE 0.04) and 8% after placebo (SE 0.02). Cohen’s d is 0.62.

IQ, predicted from study potency

Adolescent-onset persistent cannabis users in Dunedin lost 8 IQ points from childhood to age 38. DEA-seized flower over 1995–2010 averaged 7.1% THC. That is the study rate on this chart.

Psychosis, dependence, and anger

Published studies, not the state data above. Each number is from the paper cited in its row of psych_anger_studies.csv, with the sentence it comes from. Almost all of it is observational: heavy use goes with psychosis and violence, and part of that runs the other way, from early illness or temperament to use.

A · Psychosis risk

People who used high-potency cannabis every day had 4.8 times the odds of a first psychotic episode

Interval excludes 1×Interval includes 1×

Y · Use patternX · Adjusted odds ratio, log scale

Measured. Di Forti 2019 compared 901 patients with a first psychotic episode against 1,237 population controls at 11 sites in Europe and Brazil, 2010–2015. Ratios are fully adjusted; the unadjusted ratio for daily use was 6.2. Marconi 2016 pools earlier studies. Red intervals exclude 1×. Odds ratios show association; people prone to psychosis may also be drawn to cannabis.

B · Share of cases

In Ontario, the share of new schizophrenia cases tied to cannabis use disorder rose from 3.7% before legalization to 10.3% after it

OntarioDenmarkEuropean sites, high-potency useLighter bar = earlier period

Y · Place and periodX · Share of new cases attributable to cannabis, %

Measured inputs, modeled share. A population-attributable fraction is the share of cases that would not occur if the exposure were causal and removed. Ontario’s total schizophrenia rate stayed stable over the period, while psychosis not otherwise specified rose 83.7% after legalization (Myran 2025). Denmark’s since-2010 bar is the midpoint of the published 6–8% range.

C · Lasting illness

About 47% of people treated for cannabis-induced psychosis in Denmark were later diagnosed with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder

Y · Starting diagnosisX · Later diagnosed, %

Measured. Danish national registers followed people after a hospital diagnosis of substance-induced psychosis. The rate after cannabis was the highest of any substance in Starzer 2018. Murrie 2020 pools six studies.

D · Dependence and withdrawal

About 1 in 5 people who use cannabis has a use disorder, and 71.9% of frequent users in withdrawal report hostility

Use disorderWithdrawalAnger symptoms in withdrawal

Y · MeasureX · Percent

Measured. Meta-analyses and US national surveys. The first criterion for cannabis withdrawal in DSM-5 is irritability, anger, or aggression. Withdrawal is more common the heavier the use: 17% of regular users in the general population, 87% of inpatients.

E · Anger after stopping

Withdrawal irritability and aggression start within 1–3 days of stopping, peak by day 6, and fade within about 4 weeks

Y · MeasureX · Days since last use

Measured. Budney 2003 tracked symptoms daily through 45 days of abstinence. Kouri 1999 measured aggressive responding in a laboratory task, which rose on days 3 and 7 and returned to the pre-withdrawal level by day 28. Hirvonen 2012 imaged brain CB1 receptors. Small samples.

F · Violence

Across studies, people who used cannabis had about 2 to 9 times the odds of violence

Interval excludes 1×Interval includes 1×

Y · Study and groupX · Odds ratio, log scale

Measured. Schoeler 2016 followed 411 South London men; continued use from 18 to 48 predicted later violence, and earlier violence also predicted use, so the link runs both ways. The meta-analyses include studies with and without adjustment; the adjusted-only estimate is shown separately.

G · US teens

Teens who attacked someone to seriously hurt them were 3.1 times as likely to have used marijuana in the past month

Y · Behavior in the past yearX · Used marijuana in the past month, %

Measured. NSDUH 2012 detailed table 3.23B, ages 12–17. The table gives marijuana use among teens who did or did not do each thing; it does not show which came first.

H · After legalization

Whole-population studies after legalization found smaller, mixed changes: two significant rises in psychosis visits, and no significant change in psychosis diagnoses or assault injuries

Interval excludes 1×Interval includes 1×

Y · Outcome and studyX · Rate ratio after vs before, log scale

Measured. Elser 2023 and Matthay 2021 use US commercial and Medicare Advantage claims, where 77% of Elser’s follow-up time was people 65 and older, the group least likely to use. Wang 2022 is per added recreational dispensary per 10,000 residents in Colorado counties. Myran 2023 compares Ontario’s commercial-store period with before legalization; for ages 19–24 the ratio was 1.63. Matthay 2021’s only significant change was in self-harm injuries among men under 40.

Stress hormones, serotonin, and receptors

Cortisol and CB1 receptor changes are measured in human users. Serotonin changes in humans rest on one small cell study, with the mechanism shown in mice.

SystemWhat was foundStudyStrength

This figure shows co-occurrence of area-level use with area-level vote share, and the published split of industry contributions to candidates and parties. It does not show intent, coordination, a deliberate strategy, or that substance use changes any individual’s vote.

Methods

I joined SAMHSA’s 2021–2023 NSDUH substate small-area estimates to 2024 presidential votes reallocated to ZCTAs by the land-cover method (Harvard Dataverse 10.7910/DVN/Z8TSH3), with ACS 2019–2023 age and education and Census 2020 ZCTA internal points. The unit is the substate region. Weights are two-party votes. Standard errors are HC1. The specified model is the rate, log population density, percent ages 18–25, and percent ages 12–17. Ages 12–14 are three-fifths of the ACS 10–14 band, and age 25 is one-fifth of the 25–29 band.

Alaska and Hawaii have no rows in the vote file. The shapefile has 393 regions. Nebraska is in it: five regions, FIPS 31. The file’s state name on those rows says New Jersey. One New Jersey region, Southern, FIPS 34, is labeled New York. State indicators use the FIPS code. The estimation sample is 49 jurisdictions: 48 states plus the District of Columbia.

The NSDUH rates are small-area estimates. No public file links one person’s use to that person’s ballot. The slope that remains after density and age is the residual association of the rate. Past-month cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine, hallucinogens, opioid misuse, and pain-reliever misuse are past-year rates in this file, and heroin is ages 18 or older. Binge alcohol is the intensity measure SAMHSA published. Mental-illness, suicide, and perceived-risk outcomes stay out of the vote regression.

SAMHSA withdrew the 2018–2020 substate estimates. The 2021 methodology guide sets 2021 as the baseline after the move to web and in-person collection. The 2021–2023 file is one pooled period. 2018–2020 withdrawal. 2021 methodology.

User and non-user shares are the vote-weighted regression of Democratic two-party share on the rate, log density, and age, with density and age held at their vote-weighted means, then restricted to 0–100. A rate whose Duncan–Davis bounds run from 0 to 100 stays off that chart and remains on the slope panels. The contour is a vote-weighted local linear fit, tricube kernel, span 45% of the panel’s two-party votes, at least 12 regions. Low, medium, and high are vote-weighted terciles of log density.

Group A is marijuana, hallucinogens, alcohol, and cocaine. Group B is opioid misuse, pain-reliever misuse, and methamphetamine. Each region enters once per substance. The test is the interaction of the rate with group B. Controls are log density and the two age shares, centered at their vote-weighted means. Marijuana: Kloft and colleagues, 300 μg of THC per kilogram, suggested false detail 19% versus 8% on placebo. Hallucinogens: Nichols, Pharmacological Reviews, 2016, 10.1124/pr.115.011478. LSD: Carhart-Harris and colleagues, Psychopharmacology, 2015, 10.1007/s00213-014-3714-z. Alcohol expectancy: Assefi and Garry, 2003; van Oorsouw, Merckelbach, and Smeets, 2015. Cocaine: Volkow and colleagues, Nature, 1997, 10.1038/386827a0, 60–77% of dopamine transporter sites occupied at 0.3–0.6 mg/kg intravenous. Opioids: Pathan and Williams, British Journal of Pain, 2012, 10.1177/2049463712438493. Methamphetamine: Cruickshank and Dyer, Addiction, 2009, 10.1111/j.1360-0443.2009.02564.x, arousal at 5–30 mg.

A marijuana window is dropped when it asks for a 2020 or 2021 pool or would average an interview-mode pool with a web-mode pool. NAEP years 2003 through 2024 stay in the score. Current is the pool ending when the exposure window ends. Past 1 year is the pool ending the year before that. At a lag of 0, current is the pool in the NAEP year. The 5-year and 15-year lines are means of the published overlapping two-year pools in that span. Scores are population-weighted z-scores within each NAEP year. Each grade’s composite is the mean of that grade’s mathematics and reading z-scores. Weights are the ages-12-or-older population in the NAEP year. Partial r residualizes the exposure and the score on log density, percent ages 18–25, percent ages 12–17, and bachelor’s share. Those controls do not change over time. Median household income is not in the region file. Alaska and Hawaii are absent from it. The birth-to-age-5 line is adult state use, ages 12 or older, over pool end years t−14 through t−9 for grade 8 students tested in year t. CSV: marijuana_score_correlations.csv.

The suggestibility curve is linear on the logit between placebo and the Kloft dose, placed at 14% THC: half a gram of flower, 30% of the THC inhaled, 21 mg. Past that dose the band adds 35% uncertainty on the extra climb. The IQ curve multiplies the 8-point Dunedin loss by potency divided by 7.1%. Sampling error on the anchor is 2.5 points. Past 7.1% the band adds 50% uncertainty on the extra loss. Dots are measured. The rest of each curve is a prediction.

Child contrasts that publish a point difference are on the chart, in standard deviations. IQ-point results are the published points divided by 15. ABCD microdata are not used. Pittsburgh, Ottawa, and Generation R state a direction and do not state a point difference, so they are not on the chart. Paul et al., 10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2020.2902. Flak et al., 10.1111/acer.12214. Yang and Kramer, 10.1093/ije/dys071. Raman, Prasad, and Appaya, 10.4103/0019-5545.74313.

Dworak, Revelle, and Condon, Intelligence, 2023, 10.1016/j.intell.2023.101734. Table 1 publishes −0.023 SD per year. Figure 1 draws yearly means by education and does not print them. The supplement and osf.io/kmgx8 do not print them either. Those means stay off the NAEP chart. The ICAR figure on this page is that published slope, not a correlation of use with a line drawn from it.

Vote join: NSDUH 2021–2023 substate small-area estimates, SAMHSA shapefile SubstateRegionData212223, and 2024 presidential votes reallocated to ZCTAs by land cover, Harvard Dataverse 10.7910/DVN/Z8TSH3, with age and education from the ACS 2019–2023 5-year file. Alaska and Hawaii are absent from the vote file.

Shapefile outcome list: SAMHSA, 2021–2023 substate region shapefile description. Thirty-nine outcomes. Use rates and disorder rates entered above are the ones in that list.

Suggestibility and IQ: Kloft et al., PNAS 2020, 10.1073/pnas.1920162117. Meier et al., PNAS 2012, 10.1073/pnas.1206820109. Potency series: NIDA / University of Mississippi analyses of DEA-seized cannabis, 1995–2022. The vote regression, the Kloft rates, the Gawrylowicz rates, and the Dunedin 8-point loss are measured. The two potency curves are predictions.
